title: Problem decomposition and algorithm design for C programs
learningObjectives: Explain the concept and its constraints.
Trace the example and reason about its data flow.
Identify complexity, boundary or safety considerations.
Apply the concept in a tested C program.

understand.concept: Algorithm design starts by defining inputs, outputs, constraints and edge cases. Decomposition divides the problem into smaller operations with explicit responsibilities before selecting C data structures and implementation details.
understand.whyItMatters: Writing code before understanding the problem often hides assumptions and produces fragile control flow. A clear algorithm makes testing and complexity analysis possible.
understand.analogy: Treat an algorithm or data structure as a set of operations that must preserve a clearly stated contract.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace formal complexity analysis, C object rules or algorithm preconditions.

explain.narrative:
Algorithm design starts by defining inputs, outputs, constraints and edge cases. Decomposition divides the problem into smaller operations with explicit responsibilities before selecting C data structures and implementation details.

Before implementation, state input constraints, empty-case behaviour, ownership and invariants. Compile with warnings and test representative, boundary and failure cases.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: The function implements a simple algorithm: inspect each element once and count values greater than zero. Its contract should define whether values may be NULL when count is nonzero.

practise.guidedTask: Write the input, output, assumptions and edge cases for this function.
practise.independentTask: Design a program that summarizes daily sales. Decompose input validation, aggregation and report generation into separate functions.
hints: Choose data structures after identifying operations and constraints.
Use examples and boundary cases before implementation.
